content: The Duplessis Orphans were a group of children in Quebec, Canada, who were falsely diagnosed as mentally ill by the provincial government and subsequently confined to psychiatric institutions. This scheme, which occurred between the 1940s and 1960s, was orchestrated by Quebec Premier Maurice Duplessis in collaboration with the Roman Catholic Church, which managed the orphanages. The primary motivation behind this was financial, as mental institutions received federal funding, whereas orphanages and schools were solely funded by the provincial government. Many of these children were born to unwed mothers and abandoned. In some cases, Catholic orphanages were reclassified as healthcare facilities, while in others, children were transferred to existing psychiatric asylums. These children endured severe mistreatment, including physical and sexual abuse, at the hands of psychiatrists, priests, nuns, and administrators. Survivors later reported being subjected to forced labor, medical experimentation, and extreme physical punishment for perceived misbehavior. The abuse bore similarities to the atrocities committed in Catholic-run Magdalene Asylums. By the 1990s, approximately 3,000 survivors of this system formed a group called the Duplessis Orphans to campaign for justice. They uncovered falsified medical records that had labeled them as mentally deficient, which had facilitated their confinement and exploitation. Many of these children were used in drug testing and other unethical medical experiments. Upon reaching adulthood, they were released without education or life skills, leaving them ill-equipped to function in society. This led to high rates of suicide, criminal behavior, and other forms of dysfunction among the survivors. Initially, the Quebec government resisted their demands for accountability. However, after gaining widespread public attention in 1999, the government offered a token compensation of $1,000 per victim, which was widely criticized and rejected. In 2001, the government increased the offer to $10,000 per person, with an additional $1,000 for each year of wrongful confinement. This amounted to an average of $15,000 per orphan but excluded compensation for victims of sexual or other forms of abuse. Faced with limited options, eligible survivors accepted the offer, while others received nothing. The process was overseen by Bruno Roy, a former orphan who had managed to build a successful career despite his traumatic past. The settlement was later contested by those who believed the victims deserved more substantial compensation. Critics pointed out that bureaucrats processing the compensation applications were earning over $1,000 per day, while the orphans received the same amount for an entire year of illegal confinement. Additionally, the lawyer and public relations agent for the Duplessis Orphans Committee, Carlo Tarini, reportedly earned millions, further highlighting the disparity between the victims and those profiting from their plight. In 1942, the Quebec Legislative Assembly passed a law allowing the Roman Catholic Church to sell the unclaimed bodies of orphans to medical schools. This practice continued into the 1960s. In 2004, members of the Duplessis Orphans requested the government to exhume an abandoned cemetery in Montreal, which they believed contained the remains of orphans who had been subjected to medical experiments. Testimonies from individuals who had been confined at the Cité de St. Jean de Dieu asylum, now known as Louis-Hippolyte Lafontaine Hospital, indicated that many orphans were routinely experimented upon and died as a result. The group demanded that the government exhume the bodies to conduct autopsies and uncover the truth about these alleged experiments.
